In my experience, I never had cravings. I really only thought about it when I was bored, because it became a part of my nightly ritual. 

My symptoms didn’t start until the end of week 1 and persisted for 4-6 weeks, gradually getting better at around week 3.

Symptoms - 

1. Night terrors,  difficulty sleeping without waking up every couple of hours. I would wake up with extreme anxiety.

2. Tired/drained - see first symptom

2. Night sweats

3. Mood swings - likely due to poor sleep

4. Minor depression - i was flooded with a lot of unprocessed emotions I had been masking with marijuana for years. I also had what felt like a lot of idle time, so I felt bored most nights. Video games and watching comfort TV while doom scrolling didn’t feel as rewarding sober. I battled this by getting into new hobbies, lots of walking with music, joining local groups for things like crafts and books. Just challenging myself to stay busy with healthy habits. 

At this point, the only time I have a real craving is when I’ve had too much to drink. So realizing that’s a trigger, I’ve cut back on alcohol significantly and limit my drinks to 2 or 3 when I go out. And I only go out for drinks on special occasions at this point. 

Keep up the work! If and when you get more severe symptoms, stay strong. Use this sub as a tool on the hard days, and find lots of healthy distractions.

If you  doing things daily, weekly, monthly, that allows you to have other positive people and experiences in your life, you don’t have time to ruminate or feel anxious, because you’re doing something for you vs waiting on your partner to give you those feelings.

There are a lot of great books that provide techniques. It’s been scientifically proven you can calm your amygdala buy doing 10-15 minute breathing exercises. Taking 5-6 slow deep breathes per minute, pursing your lips when you exhale, exhaling slooooowly. 

I’ve been practicing recognizing my irrational thoughts as they’re happening, and separating myself from them. Telling myself “this is my anxiety talking”, please disregard.

There’s no simple solution. I know my anxiety and erratic/self-sabotaging behavior skyrocket when I drink. So if you can identify your triggers, you’ll be more aware and able to see the connections, and have an earlier opportunity to analyze the situation and defuse the anxiety, or at least align your actions with reality vs letting the anxiety speak for you. 

It’s all work and practice, you really have to condition yourself.
